method: Fix the rule before computing any role: for each kind the evaluations that speak to it with a weight and a direct or proxy mark, one ladder, the base gain, the frequency and stakes factors and the price premium, all written in role_tier_metrics.csv; read only the public numbers already in the registry (no new lookup); compute the table once; if the rule looks wrong say so and do not retune.
criteria: Included: evaluations of the independent board already read on 2026-11-10 (tier_public_scores.csv) and the list prices in tier_prices.csv, for the models that fill the four tiers. Excluded: any number not in the registry, vendor-reported tables, our own case sets as a decider (they stay as a note on a row).
sources: the hub registry files tier_public_scores.csv and tier_prices.csv (public rows checked 2026-11-10); the earlier review inv-2026-11-10-tier-public-evaluations for the grade of each evaluation

synthesis_known: Nine public evaluations of one independent board speak to the kinds of call, directly for tool and workflow completion, non-hallucination, agentic and long-horizon work, repository changes and expert-judged work products, by proxy for expert reasoning and for classification (no public evaluation measures classification on current models). question: How should a terminal arm be measured on how its screen is drawn, with public sources that can be checked, and may a model judge it?
decision: adopt a deterministic layer 1 (named checks over an emulated screen) as the ranking number after the correctness gate; adopt a model-judged layer 2 as advisory only, built and calibrated but not run on any arm; adopt the Agent Client Protocol with an external terminal client as a separate arm
method: Fix the checks, their bounds and their weights before any arm is scored; open each published source and read the claim from the page; install the external client in a scratch folder and read its own help for the launch form; write down what a model-judged review is known to miss before building one.
criteria: Included: the protocol specification, the licence of every library the metric or the arm would import or launch, the published guidelines the layer 2 checklist is drawn from, and published studies of model-judged usability evaluation. Excluded: vendor marketing pages and any claim about a terminal client that was not read in its own repository or help output.
sources: opened pages and package metadata; ran the client's own help in a scratch install
queries: opened | https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.16345 | 2026-11-11 | 1; opened | https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02306 | 2026-11-11 | 1; opened | https://agentclientprotocol.com/protocol/overview | 2026-11-11 | 1; opened | https://github.com/batrachianai/toad | 2026-11-11 | 1; opened | https://pypi.org/project/pyte/ | 2026-11-11 | 1; opened | https://pypi.org/project/agent-client-protocol/ | 2026-11-11 | 1; opened | https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ten-usability-heuristics/ | 2026-11-11 | 1; opened | https://clig.dev/ | 2026-11-11 | 1; opened | https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/articles/guidelines-for-human-ai-interaction-eighteen-best-practices-for-human-centered-ai-design/ | 2026-11-11 | 1; ran | toad acp --help in a scratch install | 2026-11-11 | 1
synthesis_known: Two published studies of model-judged usability evaluation disagree on how much a model finds: one measured that GPT-4o found 21.2% of the issues experts found with false positives from speculation (arXiv 2506.16345), the other that a multimodal model found 73% and 77% of the issues across two apps, more than five experienced evaluators (arXiv 2507.02306). Both agree it is weaker on interaction conventions and on problems that span screens. The Agent Client Protocol is JSON-RPC 2.0 with an agent run as a subprocess of the client, sessions, prompts, cancellation, permission requests and extension by underscore methods. Toad is AGPL-3.0, is run as its own program and launches an agent from a command (`toad acp COMMAND PATH`). pyte is LGPL-3.0 and the Python SDK for the protocol is Apache-2.0 by its packaged licence file.
synthesis_contested: The studies disagree on direction, so neither supports trusting a model to judge a terminal screen: both measured screens of graphical apps (not text grids), with different models, prompts and expert panels; whether a judge on a text frame with a quoted-evidence rule does better is not known until it is calibrated.
synthesis_unknown: How a model judge behaves on text grids of terminal screens; how the external client draws a hub session beyond one scripted launch; whether Toad's terminal rendering can be captured by the same emulator without a person (one launch was tried); the contrast a terminal really draws for faint text (it varies by terminal).
limitations: Both studies are abstracts read on 2026-11-11 (the papers were not read in full), on graphical apps. The SDK's licence is not stated on its PyPI page and was read from the LICENSE file in the installed wheel. WCAG success criterion 1.4.3 (4.5:1) is cited from the standard and was not opened today. pyte has had no release since November 2023. Layer 2 was built and its calibration set frozen but not run on any arm, by decision: a live arm is never run just to fill a row.
decisions: Layer 1 deterministic metric: adopt: the emulated screen is free, repeatable and reads what the person sees; Layer 2 model-judged review: adopt as advisory only: the published evidence is mixed and from other kinds of screen, so it is measured on injected defects first and never gates; pyte for evaluation only: adopt: LGPL-3.0, imported by the evaluation folder and never by the hub package; Toad: adopt as a separate arm run as its own program: AGPL-3.0 allows it only that way; Agent Client Protocol SDK: adopt as an optional extra: Apache-2.0

question: What must a hub adapter implement to be driven by a terminal client through the Agent Client Protocol, which hub-specific information can and cannot cross that protocol, which clients exist, and what public guidance exists on terminal and agent interface quality?
decision: Whether to build the protocol arm of terminal-session (the hub as an agent, an external client drawing it) beside the arm that moves the consumer's polished screen into the hub, and what the metric that picks the arm bare ahohs opens must and must not claim. Extends inv-2026-11-11-terminal-presentation-metric, which holds the usability studies, Toad licence and install, pyte, the heuristics and the SDK licence; this record holds only what that one lacks.
method: Read the protocol's own pages for transport, tool calls, permission requests, cancel, extension and the prompt turn; read the repositories of the protocol and its Python SDK and the client's repository; read the client directory as a list of candidates, not as proof; read the hub's own ACP client code to see which side it already speaks; mark every point a page did not state as unverified instead of filling it.
criteria: Included: the protocol specification pages, the maintainer repositories, the one terminal client built on Textual, and public guidance on terminal and agent interface quality. Excluded: blog explainers as the source of any protocol fact, and any client whose licence or rendering was not read at its own repository.
sources: opened pages; web search; read the hub's own source
queries: opened | https://agentclientprotocol.com/protocol/v1/transports | 2026-11-11 | 1; opened | https://agentclientprotocol.com/protocol/tool-calls | 2026-11-11 | 1; opened | https://agentclientprotocol.com/protocol/prompt-turn | 2026-11-11 | 1; opened | https://agentclientprotocol.com/protocol/extensibility | 2026-11-11 | 1; opened | https://github.com/agentclientprotocol/agent-client-protocol | 2026-11-11 | 1; opened | https://github.com/agentclientprotocol/python-sdk | 2026-11-11 | 1; opened | https://agentclientprotocol.com/get-started/clients | 2026-11-11 | 1; opened | https://github.com/batrachianai/toad | 2026-11-11 | 1; web search | Toad custom ACP agent launch command | 2026-11-11 | 16; web search | Agent Client Protocol maintainers and transport | 2026-11-11 | 20; web search | LLM-as-judge UI screenshot usability heuristic evaluation reliability | 2026-11-11 | 10; observed | the hub's ACP client files under the_world/tools/delegated_agent_sessions | 2026-11-11 | 4
screened_out: 4 secondary explainer pages that name the protocol's originators (blog posts, not the specification); 3 clients from the community directory whose licence and rendering were not read (Martty, SpurCode, Nori CLI)
synthesis_known: The protocol is JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio, with the agent run as a subprocess of the client; stdio is the only transport defined, newline-delimited; a remote Streamable HTTP transport is in a separate proposal and custom transports are allowed. A tool call has an id, a title, a kind (read, edit, delete, move, search, execute, think, fetch, switch_mode, other), a status (pending, in_progress, completed, failed), content (text, diff, terminal) and locations that are display data only. A permission request offers allow_once, allow_always, reject_once, reject_always and returns selected or cancelled. Cancel is a notification, the agent must end the prompt with stop reason cancelled, and pending permission requests are answered cancelled. Extension is by _meta, underscore-prefixed custom methods and reverse-DNS capability keys. The protocol's repository is Apache-2.0 with libraries in five languages; the Python SDK is Apache-2.0 and has agent and client sides. The hub already has an ACP client (it drives an agent as a harness and sends a steering extension) and no agent side. Toad is a Python and Textual terminal under AGPL-3.0 that renders streaming markdown and diffs and starts an agent from a command.
synthesis_contested: Whether a typed line during a run can reach the agent: the pages read describe no message sent during a turn (only cancel), so steering depends on a custom method that a stock client may not send. Whether a model judging text frames does better than the studies of graphical screens: the evidence points both ways and a newer paper argues screenshot-only judging is weakly grounded (read as a snippet only).
synthesis_unknown: Who maintains the protocol (no page read names them; secondary sources say Zed and JetBrains, not verified). Whether Toad shows a helper tree, a header of spend against ceilings or a collapsible structure view (the protocol has no field for a helper's parent or for a structure tree). Whether Toad has a configuration file for custom agents (only the command form was confirmed). The licences and rendering of the other terminal clients in the directory. Whether Terminal-Bench or any other public benchmark scores terminal interface quality (searched from memory, not looked up in this pass, so none is claimed).
limitations: The directory of clients is community-written and says some entries only connect or adjoin the protocol, so it is not proof that each is a client. One search returned only snippets for the OpenHands page, the newer benchmark paper and the practitioner critique. The Python SDK repository page showed an empty releases section while the registry record for the package names version 1.0.0, so the version is taken from the earlier record. Mapping of the hub's events to protocol messages is a reading of the specification and of the hub's contract, not a run. The consumer's terminal size and rule inventory belongs to a separate port review and is not recorded here.
decisions: Protocol arm: adopt as a separate arm, the hub run as an agent over stdio and the client launched as its own program: the specification allows it and the licence only permits launching; Protocol arm as the owner of hub-specific information: reject: the protocol has no field for a helper's parent, a structure tree or a ceilings header, so those arrive as text or _meta that a stock client may ignore and the metric must count that as a protocol limit, apart from a drawing fault; Steering through the protocol: defer: no documented mid-turn message, a custom method until the client's behaviour is read; Other terminal clients from the directory: defer: licence and rendering not read; Model-judged review: keep advisory, as the earlier record decided

question: Which open-source terminal agent interface, in any language, is best finished, and by what route could the hub's sessions (typed events and controls, and its ACP agent) be drawn by it?
decision: choose which stock terminal interface the hub serves a protocol to as its first screen arm (a separate program for each, or a fork of its interface code), so the hub stops hand-writing its own terminal screens
method: Fix the criteria and the licence rule before reading: a candidate is kept only if its licence file is read and it is open source in the usual sense; list the candidates from the owner's brief, a search for comparisons and the ACP clients directory; read each candidate's source in a shallow clone (licence, interface toolkit, how the interface reaches an agent, protocol size and documentation); read release dates and counts through the GitHub API; mark a point not verified when no source read it; launch no candidate that needs an account.
criteria: Included: open source by licence file, a terminal interface (not a desktop or web app), maintained with a release or push in the last three months, a documented or readable route by which an outside server can be drawn (an attach option, a published protocol, or a client of ACP). Excluded: proprietary or source-available licences, deprecated interfaces, projects with no route to draw a foreign agent. Judged on evidence of the screen, maturity and maintenance, independent reviews and adoption; stars alone do not decide.
sources: web search; opened pages (agentclientprotocol.com clients directory, opencode docs for server and API, ampcode manual); shallow source clones read (opencode, codex, mistral-vibe, crush, goose, gemini-cli, pi); GitHub API for licence, stars, push date and releases
queries: web search | best open source terminal AI coding agent TUI comparison 2026 | 2026-11-11 | 17; web search | Mistral Vibe 3 Rust terminal interface announcement app-server | 2026-11-11 | 18; web search | opencode TUI vs Codex CLI vs Crush terminal UI quality flicker scrolling review | 2026-11-11 | 17; opened | agentclientprotocol.com get-started clients | 2026-11-11 | 1; opened | opencode.ai docs server, llms.txt and api | 2026-11-11 | 3; opened | ampcode.com manual | 2026-11-11 | 1; source clones | opencode, codex, mistral-vibe, crush, goose, gemini-cli, pi | 2026-11-11 | 7; github api | licence, stars, push date and releases of repositories | 2026-11-11 | 18
screened_out: 7 ACP terminal clients listed in the directory and not read (acpx, Hydra, Orca CLI, pool, Intelligent Terminal, SpurCode, acp-runner); 2 named only in search results and not examined (DeepSeek TUI, Ralph TUI)
change_my_mind: a spike in which the stock client of the first arm refuses a stub server on a call the stub cannot reasonably answer, or the presentation metric scores its screen below the hub's own
synthesis_known: Three open interfaces are clients of a published protocol and can be pointed at a server the hub provides: opencode (MIT, TypeScript on OpenTUI and Solid, a server option, an HTTP API with 170 operations and 499 schemas and 97 event types), Mistral Vibe 3 (Apache-2.0, Rust ratatui, newline-delimited JSON-RPC on stdio, a 521-line protocol reference, an environment variable replaces the server command) and Codex (Apache-2.0, Rust ratatui, a remote option over websocket or unix socket, committed JSON Schema of 109 requests, 86 notifications and 10 server requests). Only opencode's interface has a client plugin path with slots (sidebar, home, footer, prompt) that adds panels without a fork. The Vibe repository carries a pseudo-terminal harness with pyte and committed screen goldens in 95 scenario folders. Crush is FSL-1.1-MIT (competing use barred, MIT after two years), Claude Code is all rights reserved, Goose's terminal interface is deprecated, and Gemini CLI and Pi showed no route to draw a foreign server. Kiro CLI is closed source (AWS Intellectual Property License), its Amazon Q ancestor repository (Apache-2.0 and MIT files, Rust, inline prompt libraries) is frozen, and its terminal interface is an ACP client of its own harness with no documented route to a foreign agent. Interface style from source or documentation: inline by default only in Gemini CLI (alternate screen opt-in); both in Claude Code (classic or fullscreen, default depends on setup), Kiro CLI (inline with a /fullscreen toggle, default not stated), Codex (alternate screen by default, --no-alt-screen) and opencode (main interface full-screen, the mini command inline with a footer); full-screen only found in Mistral Vibe v3 and Crush; Toad unverified. Claude Code can show hub information without a fork: a status line command (session JSON with cost, context and rate limits, any lines, refreshed on events and a timer), 33 settings hook events (a systemMessage to the user, context for Claude, permission block, run stop), sub-agents by file or --agents, output styles, append-system-prompt flags, plugins, and mods (a pane or band, transcript rows, a line under each answer, commands) that run inside it with the user's permissions.
synthesis_contested: Which screen is best finished: no head-to-head test was read, only anecdotes (one commenter finds opencode scrolling glitchy, comparison pages praise Crush, one page wrongly says opencode uses Bubble Tea while its source shows OpenTUI) and adoption (opencode 226203 stars, Codex 134941, Vibe 5371), which is not finish. How stable each protocol is: opencode labels its HTTP API experimental and its event stream volatile, the Vibe reference says the dispatcher still has coupling, Codex gates parts behind an experimental flag.
synthesis_unknown: Whether any stock client draws a third-party server without error (none was launched); the smallest subset of each protocol a stub must answer; how each screen renders under pyte; how well sub-agents, the todo list, diffs and cost are drawn on screen; the licence of Amp; the Codex release count for three months.
limitations: No candidate was installed or launched, so no screen was seen and none compared. Sources are shallow clones read at their 2026-11-11 heads. The opencode API documentation page was read for its first 100000 of 266318 characters. Method counts come from committed schema files and greps of source, not from running the clients. Comparison pages found by search are mostly affiliate or machine-written. The ACP directory lists twelve terminal clients and only five were read. Adapter sizes quoted in the report are estimates. For the interface-feel question no head-to-head comparison of opencode or Mistral Vibe with Claude Code or Kiro CLI was found, only one Hacker News thread of 2025 and comparison pages, so whether either matches their quality is unproven. The Claude Code documentation pages were read through a summarising fetch and the hooks page only in part. Mods are documented as of Claude Code v2.1.290 and later, and the hub has not tried one.
decisions: opencode V2 terminal interface through its server option: build-on: first arm, the hub serves the opencode HTTP API as a separate program and adds hub panels as client plugins, after a one-day spike with a stub server shows the stock client accepts it; Mistral Vibe v3 Rust interface through its server command variable: adapt: second arm, the hub serves the Vibe app-server protocol using the vendored protocol models and forks the Rust crate only for panels the protocol cannot carry; Codex CLI interface through its remote option: defer: the protocol is large and tied to account and model flows so run it only if the first two fail the presentation metric; Crush: reject: FSL-1.1-MIT bars competing use and its Go packages are internal so only a fork could draw the hub; Toad: defer: AGPL-3.0 so a separate program only, as the earlier record decided; Gemini CLI: reject: no route found to draw a foreign agent, only to act as an ACP agent; Goose: reject: its terminal interface is deprecated and its source removed; Pi: reject: its rpc mode drives Pi and does not draw a foreign server; Nori CLI: defer: a small ACP client with 194 stars, and since the hub already serves ACP it is a free extra screen to score; Martty: defer: sources disagree on its toolkit and it has 82 stars; Hash: reject: a shell with agent help, not a coding session screen; Raven: reject: a host that plans work, not a screen for another agent; Claude Code as source to fork: reject: proprietary licence; Claude Code as the screen through its extension points (status line, settings hooks, plugins and mods, sub-agents, output styles, Agent SDK): defer: it adds hub lines and panels to Claude Code's own run and cannot draw a hub session started elsewhere, so it is a comparison screen to score and not an arm; Kiro CLI: reject: closed source under the AWS Intellectual Property License and no route found to draw a foreign agent; Amp: reject: no open licence found on the pages read; Aider and Qwen Code and Kilo Code and Cline: defer: not examined for a server route

question: Which open-source terminal agent or chat interfaces have code that could be the starting point of the hub's terminal (vendored or forked into an Apache-2.0 Python library), which can only be run as a separate program, and how could each be compared by the presentation metric?
decision: build one new arm from the best permissively licensed Python interface code, driven by the hub's session events and controls and scored on the presentation metric and the session gate, instead of writing screens from scratch; score separate-program clients through a pseudo-terminal
method: State the criteria before reading any candidate: licence compatible with Apache-2.0, Python, a Textual or Rich or prompt_toolkit screen, and a UI layer that does not import its agent loop. Read each candidate's licence file, language, last release and push date from its repository record; install the two best Python candidates in scratch virtual environments (never the hub's) and read their UI source to count lines and list what the UI imports; download one more source tag where the installed package was an older version; open the protocol's client and agent lists for the separate-program clients. No candidate was run against a model.
criteria: Included: a licence file of Apache-2.0, MIT or BSD that allows vendoring into an Apache-2.0 library, with a Python UI built on Textual, Rich or prompt_toolkit and a UI layer that can be separated from its agent loop (for code), or a documented protocol the hub can serve (for a separate program). Excluded: copyleft or source-available licences for code reuse, UI that is part of the agent loop, interfaces with no tool-call, permission or plan display, and projects no longer Python.
sources: opened pages and repository records; installed two candidates in scratch virtual environments and read their source
queries: opened | https://agentclientprotocol.com/get-started/clients | 2026-11-11 | 12; opened | https://agentclientprotocol.com/get-started/agents | 2026-11-11 | 10; opened | https://opencode.ai/docs/acp/ | 2026-11-11 | 1; opened | https://textual.textualize.io/widgets/markdown/ | 2026-11-11 | 1; opened | repository records of each candidate (licence, language, stars, last push) | 2026-11-11 | 29; ran | installed mistral-vibe 2.26.1 and 3.1.2 and the openhands package in scratch virtual environments and read their UI source | 2026-11-11 | 3; opened | OpenHands CLI 1.16.0 source tag and Mistral Vibe changelog and repository tree | 2026-11-11 | 2

synthesis_known: Mistral Vibe release v2.26.1 is the only candidate that is Apache-2.0, Python, Textual, complete (streamed markdown, tool-call rows, diff, approval and question screens, todo status, subagent transcripts, session picker, status line, themes) and separated from its agent: none of its 98 UI files imports its core package, they import only an app-server layer of about 4,400 lines (events, models, protocol, session). Mistral replaced that Textual UI with a Rust CLI in v3.0.0 (2026-10-15), so the Python UI is a frozen snapshot. OpenHands CLI 1.16.0 is MIT and Textual with a smaller UI (about 6,600 lines) that renders openhands.sdk event classes, and its README says it is no longer actively maintained. Kimi CLI (legacy) is Apache-2.0, archived, with a typed event wire close to the hub's events and controls. Textual can stream markdown (MarkdownStream) and lists no chat widget. Aider, Elia, gptme and Posting are not usable as a base (UI inside the agent, no tool rows, or no longer Python). Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, opencode, Goose and Open Interpreter are not Python; Toad is AGPL-3.0 and Crush FSL-1.1-MIT. Twelve ACP clients are flagged as terminal clients on the protocol's list; opencode, Goose, Gemini CLI, Mistral Vibe, Kimi CLI, Qwen Code, OpenHands and Cline are listed as ACP agents, and Codex CLI and Claude Code through adapters.
synthesis_contested: Whether a trimmed copy of a 26,000 line UI is cheaper to own than the hub's own screens is not settled: the UI reaches its agent through a wide interface (126 model classes) that the hub's eight events and five controls do not cover, so part of the work is stubbing or deleting screens the hub has no use for.

question: How can a conversation with an AI apply the structure of a person's intent (problems, ideals, solutions with milestones and one authoritative metric, alternatives compared by that metric) so that an answer brings grounded clarity, when most people do not know the framework: what structure do the consumer's intents hold, what of it reaches a chat turn, what can a turn write, and what do the hub's records already say?
decision: specify a hub solution that decides, by code from a structured planner move and the records held, what structure a reply carries and at most one offer to keep the missing pieces; measure it on structured fields with a plain baseline arm; build it in small steps starting with the smallest change to the reply standard
method: Fixed before reading: four questions (what structure is held and how much of it is filled, what reaches a chat turn, what a turn can write and under which consent, what the hub's own solution records say about the behaviour and what is unbuilt) and one rule for what counts as a finding: it is read from the code or records themselves, quoted or counted, never from memory or from older notes. Sources are the hub's solution records and code, the consumer runner's reply standards, planner and deep-run code (paths relative to that package), the consumer backend's specification, guidance and chat code (a private repository, so named by role), the ESOI skill text, and read-only counts on one deployment's development data (counts and field coverage only, no text). Candidates are the possible designs for the behaviour; each fact is kept when it changes the design.
criteria: Included: a fact that is read from the code, the records or a count and that decides where a piece of the behaviour belongs, what exists already to reuse, or what must not be duplicated. Excluded: opinions about wording, facts about surfaces that a conversation never touches, and anything that cannot be reproduced from the sources.
sources: opened code and record files of public repositories; opened code of one private repository by role; read-only counts on one deployment's development data
queries: opened | hubofhubs/the_intelligence/critical_thinking/esoi_application/ solutions.csv, metrics.csv and apply.py | 2026-11-11 | 3; opened | hubofhubs/the_intelligence/subconscious/relevant_solutions/ solutions.csv, records_then_model.py, network.py | 2026-11-11 | 3; opened | hubofhubs/the_consciousness/ai_session_experience/structure_in_view/ solutions.csv | 2026-11-11 | 1; opened | the_intelligence/mind/response_writer/reply_standards.py and planner/orchestrator_decide_tool.py in the runner package | 2026-11-11 | 2; opened | the_intelligence/critical_thinking/goal_iteration.py and mind/delegation/orchestrator_deep_run.py in the runner package | 2026-11-11 | 2; opened | the_self/integrity/prompts/standing_instructions.py in the runner package | 2026-11-11 | 1; opened | the consumer backend's specification store, grants, guidance cards and tool documentation | 2026-11-11 | 5; counted | the consumer backend's development database, read-only | 2026-11-11 | 1
screened_out: 2 facts about screens a conversation never touches; 1 fact superseded by a later read of the same file
synthesis_known: An intent's structure is five record types (problems, ideals, solutions, implementations, metrics) with structured milestones and one authoritative metric per solution, plus rows derived from the intent's own fields; an AI may write it by ensure-one additions, a person's edited field is locked, and an AI write needs the intent's autopilot on and the person's edit grant not none (default auto with undo). In one deployment's development data nearly every intent holds an ideal and four in five a problem, about one in ten a solution and one in thirty a metric, and none holds alternatives, a milestone, a logged value or an application question; three quarters were still in creation. A chat turn receives the intent's identity, a card listing a few solution titles and retrieved guidance, but the specification slice, the relevant-solutions pass and the ESOI standing instructions reach deep runs only. Reply shapes are chosen from a structured planner field and the advice shape forbids remarks about missing records. The hub records esoi-application as an edit applier (not a decider of what a reply carries), relevant-solutions with a records_index arm selected and a records_then_model arm that works over rows from any source, and structure-in-view as the display of structure with detail one action away. A status and next-step path already composes replies from a dated snapshot that includes the key measure.
synthesis_contested: Whether structure should be written automatically in the turn or offered first: the grant default is auto with undo, while the owner's direction for this pass is offer first. Whether alternatives are best kept as implementation records or as goals: an existing flow keeps each alternative of a deliverable as a goal, the ESOI definition makes an alternative an implementation of a solution. Whether the closing paragraph can come from the single answer call.
synthesis_unknown: How often a real person accepts an offer to keep structure; whether the six terms are understood from use by people who do not know the framework; how the proportions on one deployment's development data compare with production; whether the planner's move stays stable on stronger tiers.
limitations: The counts are from one deployment's development database, much of it test data, and are proportions, not a population; production was not read. The chat's behaviour was read from code, not from a live panel of users. Nothing here measures whether structure helps a person; the metric of the solution built from this review checks that the right structure is carried, not that it helps.
decisions: A hub solution that decides the structure of a reply by code from a planner move and the records held: build-on: no seat decides which structure a reply carries, esoi-application only applies an edit, structure-in-view only displays, and a new solution has a distinct purpose, two competing arms and a metric of its own; A structured planner field with none as default instead of matching words in the message or the reply: adopt: the stay-out turns must stay plain and a word list leaks every case it did not anticipate; The relevant-solutions arm that shortlists from the records and asks one cheap model call, for the intent holding several solutions: adopt: it works over rows from any source and is already measured in the hub; The ESOI standing instructions in every chat answer call: reject: they are written for deep work, long, and teach the framework instead of the person's situation; A prompt-only change to the advice reply standard as the first step: adopt: smallest change that shows the closing paragraph and costs no new record; Offering to keep structure first and recording only after a yes: adopt: the owner's direction for this pass, and an accepted offer can be carried out by code; Automatic recording in the turn: defer: needs the measured accept rate of offers first

question: How should research done while answering be made a disciplined, recorded and reusable act behind the hub's Learning solution, and where should each part of its record live in a consumer?
decision: build one Learning arm (recorded_research) behind three ports (investigation store, knowledge sink, context sink) and measure it against the arm that returns the record without keeping it, with the consumer supplying its own store, knowledge writer and context card
method: Read what each repository already does with research before designing: the hub's review arm and store, the consumer runner's investigation tool and web adapter wiring, and the consumer backend's investigation collection, specification write gates and context cards. Fix the cases and their equal weights in the evaluation component before scoring any arm, record the baseline arm first, then score the new arm; verify on a real dev quest with the read-only chat replay.
criteria: Included: code and records in the three repositories as read on 2026-11-11, and the results of the evaluation component and the chat replay. Excluded: anything not read in the code, and any claim about real-web answer quality (the scripted cases use fixed fake results and a scripted judge).
sources: repository files read; evaluation component run offline; read-only chat replay on a dev quest
queries: read | hubofhubs/the_world/learning/systematic_review.py and investigation_store.py | 2026-11-11 | 2; read | the consumer runner's investigation tool, planner web read dispatch and web adapter wrapper | 2026-11-11 | 3; read | the consumer backend's investigation module, specification write gates and context cards | 2026-11-11 | 3; ran | research_recorded on systematic_review and recorded_research | 2026-11-11 | 2; ran | chat replay of four turns on a dev quest | 2026-11-11 | 4
screened_out: 1 reading that did not bear on the question
synthesis_known: Before this work the hub's review returned a record and wrote nothing; reuse was by exact question only and an extension became a new row. The consumer runner already placed a question on a strategy, judged reuse with one fast-tier call and recorded through the backend, but only when the planner chose its investigation tool; a plain web read neither looked up nor recorded. The backend already held investigations in one collection with fresh, partial and stale reuse states and superseding on extension, and the specification already had one AI write path with its gates (autopilot on, a person's edits locked, revisions checked). Measured offline on 30 cases with equal weights, the arm that returns the record without keeping it passed 5 and recorded_research passed 30, and the searches made on the reuse cases fell from 62 to 10. On a real dev quest a related question in a fresh conversation was answered from the earlier investigation with its date and no search, an unrelated question searched, and the same question in another quest searched and did not see the first quest's research.
synthesis_contested: Whether a plain web read should be recorded: a quick fact informs no decision and is not recorded by design, while a research ask for a plan should be. In the replay the planner answered a research ask with plain web reads and no record, and routed an explicit investigation to a background task, so recording after a plain read depends on the planner choosing the investigation tool.
synthesis_unknown: How a real judge behaves across many real questions (the scripted cases use a scripted judge); whether the knowledge write lands on strategies in quests with autopilot on (the replay quest had autopilot off and the investigation bore on the whole quest, so the findings were proposed, not written); how the context card ranks against other cards in retrieval for a related question.
limitations: The offline cases use fixed fake search results and a scripted judge. The replay used one dev quest with autopilot off, and its first investigation was seeded through the backend's own create function because the replay writes nothing. Only four replay turns were run. The hub arm is used by the runner for its lookup logic (earlier) only; the runner's own placement and tool still do the recording.
decisions: recorded_research arm: build-on: same signature as the review arm, measured 30 of 30 against 5 of 30 on the offline cases; three ports: adopt: the consumer supplies store, knowledge sink and context sink and the hub's folders are the defaults; knowledge through the specification's AI write: adopt: it keeps the existing gates and never replaces a person's text; context card per investigation: adopt: fenced by the quest's scope tag so research does not cross quests; recording after plain web reads: defer: a quick fact is not recorded and the planner must choose the investigation tool for a research ask

question: Can the stock opencode V2 terminal client (MIT, TypeScript on OpenTUI) draw a session of the hub by attaching to a small server that speaks opencode's HTTP API over the hub's Harness, which requests and events does it need, what does its own screen show at the presentation metric's sizes, and does its plugin registry carry what only the hub knows?
decision: build one Terminal Experience arm, opencode_client_session, that starts a hub-owned loopback server and launches the installed client as a separate program (full-screen or inline), with a client plugin shipped as source; not selected, because the presentation metric decides
method: Fixed before running anything: read the client's source (the connect path, the data layer that builds its screen from a snapshot and events, the permission prompt, the tool renderers, the plugin slots, the inline interface) and its OpenAPI file; install the published package into a scratch folder with all of the client's own folders redirected there and its update check and model fetch turned off; run the client against a logging server that answers every route with 404 and then against a stub that answers the routes it asked for, scripted from the hub's own session events; read each screen through the pyte terminal emulator at 100x30 and 56x24 and cross-check pyte against tmux on the same bytes; send the keys for approve, refuse, a typed note, cancel and resume through the pseudo-terminal and record what reached the server; load the smallest plugin once; then build the arm and score the real client's screen with the presentation metric.
criteria: Included: the client at version 2.2.7 from the npm package @opencode/cli and the matching source commit, run on this machine; behaviour seen on a screen or in a request log. Excluded: any claim about other versions, other platforms, a real model session, or the hosted web and desktop interfaces; the earlier research claims were treated as untested until run.
sources: client source and OpenAPI file read; npm registry metadata; runs of the client against a logging server and a stub; the presentation metric run on the real client
queries: read | the client's connect path, server info check and version warning in its command line package | 2026-11-11 | 1; read | the client's data layer events, message projection and permission prompt | 2026-11-11 | 6; read | the plugin slot map and a plugin test fixture | 2026-11-11 | 3; read | the inline interface's transport and its session wait | 2026-11-11 | 2; run | the client against a server answering every route with 404, then against the stub | 2026-11-11 | 3; run | the client in a pseudo-terminal at 100x30 and 56x24, through pyte and tmux | 2026-11-11 | 4; run | the plugin in a per-run folder | 2026-11-11 | 2
screened_out: 3 notes about the hosted and desktop interfaces; 2 notes about other protocol surfaces the client has but this arm does not use
observe: what the client requests at start and in a session; what its screen shows for each hub event; whether a plugin loads unmodified
change_my_mind: a client release that changes a route or event the arm needs; a version of the client that refuses a server reporting another version
stop: when the scripted session, the five controls and the plugin had each been seen on the real client at both sizes
synthesis_known: The client attaches with --server URL after one GET of /api/info and only warns on another version. A server needs about 33 requests and 24 event types (the OpenAPI file has 170 operations and 97 event types); several of them are experimental routes the client calls at every start, and a missing one shows as a toast. The client builds its screen from a snapshot it reads and the events that follow, so a projection store that agrees with the events is the core of a server. Every control the hub has reaches a request: a permission reply, a prompt with the client's own message id, an interrupt. The plugin registry loads a plugin from a folder given to the client, unmodified, and its slots show hub information at every width through the composer slot. The inline interface (opencode mini) needs the same routes and one more (a long poll for the session to settle) and loads no plugin.
synthesis_contested: Whether an API labelled experimental and unversioned is a safe thing to build an arm on: the client warns only on a version mismatch and the source and the binary agreed for the one version tested, but nothing pins the route shapes. Whether the client's own look (its left bar for the goal, its key hints, its spinner colours) should be scored against checks written for the hub's own header and rows.
synthesis_unknown: How the routes and events change from release to release (one version was tested); how the client behaves on reconnect with a replay gap, with several sessions or with a very large diff (not run); whether the inline interface can show anything the plugin shows (it loads no plugin); colours were checked for contrast only against the metric's rule.
limitations: One client version (2.2.7), one machine, one operating system, no model session. The stub's agent, model and provider shapes were copied from the client's own local server output (run with no model call). The screens are read through pyte (colours not cross-checked against another emulator; text cross-checked against tmux on the same bytes). The scenarios use scripted harnesses, not a real run.
decisions: opencode V2 stock terminal client: adopt: launched as a separate program, never bundled (MIT); opencode HTTP API subset served by the hub: build-on: standard library server over the Harness with the routes and events measured here; client plugin registry: adopt: one small source file shipped in package data and copied per run; inline interface (opencode mini): adopt: same server, no plugin; the unversioned API and the 258 MB client: adapt: the tested version is named in the availability message and another major version is warned about, and the person installs the client themselves

question: How should the hub of hubs integrate opencode as a hub: (a) its provider and model catalogue (75+ providers from models.dev) against the hub's vendor model caller and price table, (b) its agent loop, sub-agents, plugins and Claude route against the opencode_runner arm, (c) its terminal client as a screen arm, (d) how a person gets the client, and which metric should decide?
decision: keep the opencode terminal client as a selectable arm (offered when installed, pinned and never bundled) with the hub as its one provider and its tiers as the model list; run one fast-tier trial of opencode_runner on opencode's own Claude Agent integration before any claim about the subscription route; use models.dev as a cross-check feed for the hub's price rows, not as their source
method: Fixed before running: (1) fetch the models.dev catalogue file and compare its shape and every price row the hub holds; (2) read the hub's opencode_runner arm, its arm ideas, priors and waivers; (3) run the stock client 2.2.7 on a pseudo-terminal (tmux, 200x45) against the hub's server before and after the provider change and read what its startup panel and model picker show; (4) read the client's own program text for the rule that shows the connect-a-provider panel and for its Claude integration, then run its login and model listing in an empty scratch profile (no model call); (5) read the recorded terminal presentation results of the arm next to the other arms; (6) read the package registry entry for how the client is obtained.
criteria: Included: the client at 2.2.7 on one Linux machine, the catalogue file as fetched on 2026-11-12, the hub's own records and code, runs that make no model call. Excluded: any claim about a real model session through opencode, other client versions or platforms, the vendors' terms of use for a subscription, and opencode's hosted services.
sources: the models.dev catalogue file; the hub's price table, arm ideas, priors and waivers; the opencode_runner arm source; runs of the client on a pseudo-terminal; the client's program text; the hub's recorded presentation results; the npm registry entry of the client package

screened_out: 0 items: every item read changed or bounded a decision
observe: what the catalogue holds and whether it agrees with the hub's prices; what the client's panel and picker show for each provider answer; whether the client reaches the Claude CLI without a key; how the client arm scores against the arms the hub drew itself
change_my_mind: a trial showing opencode_runner on its Claude Agent integration cannot finish a deep-work case on the fast tier; a client release that changes the integration or session-model routes; a price check showing the catalogue wrong where the hub's rows are right on every differing row

synthesis_known: (a) The catalogue file lists 235 providers and 8998 models, each with cost per million tokens (input, output, cache read and write) and context and output limits, and 394 models carry no cost; it has an entry for every one of the 25 models in the hub's price table. Of the 24 base price rows 18 agree exactly and 6 (two providers) differ, each by exactly a factor of two, and the hub's tiered row by prompt size has no counterpart in a flat cost field. The client lists models by provider from two routes the hub already serves and shows the hub as one provider with its tiers as models. (b) opencode 2.2.7 has its own Claude Agent integration whose method is the Claude CLI login; with a logged-in CLI, connecting it needed no key and no model call. The opencode_runner arm names the provider through a small map and a model string, so a new provider id is a map entry and a tier row, not a new arm. (c) The client's connect-a-provider panel shows exactly while no integration holds a connection; serving the hub as one connected integration removes it, and a pick in the model picker arrives as a session model request the hub maps to a tier for the next run. The client arm scores 7 of 8 checks on the presentation metric against 9 of 9 for the arms the hub draws itself. (d) The client is MIT, one npm package per platform, 258 MB for the one installed here, with the latest release the tested one.
synthesis_contested: Whether the six price rows that differ are the hub's error or the catalogue's: both are a factor of two, which suggests a pricing mode (a long-context or priority price on one side) rather than a typing slip, but no vendor page was read here. Whether the unversioned, experimental server API is safe to build on: it held for the one version tested and the client warns only on a version mismatch.
synthesis_unknown: Whether opencode_runner on the Claude Agent integration completes deep-work cases, at what pass rate, cost and time (no run was made); which models that integration lists once a session runs (a standalone model listing showed none for it); whether the vendor allows a subscription to be used through a third-party harness even when it starts the vendor's own CLI; whether opencode's sub-agents, commands and skills can be fed from the hub (the server routes for commands and skills exist and the hub answers them empty; no list was served); how the catalogue changes week to week.
limitations: One client version, one machine, one operating system, no real model session. The catalogue was fetched once and compared by model id on the base rows only. The Claude integration was seen connecting, not working. The terminal presentation score of the client arm includes checks the hub's other arms were tuned to and one (colour contrast) that belongs to the client's own theme. Another agent is changing the files the presentation metric uses.
decisions: opencode stock terminal client as a terminal arm: build-on: already built and measured at 7 of 8, stays selectable, offered when the client is installed, not the default until the presentation metric ranks it first; the hub as the client's one provider with its tiers as the model list: build-on: one connected integration, three tier models, a model pick maps to the next run's tier; models.dev as the hub's provider and price source: adapt: a weekly cross-check of the hub's price rows with differences listed, never the source, because 6 of 24 rows differ and tiered prices have no field; calling providers through opencode from the vendor caller: reject: a model call would need the agent binary and its server for no gain over the thin callers; opencode_runner on the Claude Agent integration: defer: run one fast-tier deep-work trial before any claim, then record or waive it; opencode's own agent loop, sub-agents, commands and skills: defer: serve hub skills through the client's skill and command routes only if the trial shows the loop earns its place; bundling or vendoring the client: reject: it is a 258 MB binary per platform and the person installs it; pin policy: adapt: the tested version stays named in the install hint and a different major version is warned about, bump after the presentation metric and the server tests pass on the new one
